LL_BERN: log-logistic Bernoulli mixture model

Source: vignettes/llbern.Rmd
llbern.Rmd
library(bssd)

Model

The log-logistic Bernoulli (LL_BERN) model of Duncan (2026, Section 3.4) replaces the exponential distribution of EXP_BERN (vignette("expbern")) by the log-logistic distribution, so that the hazard of the event can change over time. For subject \(i\) with the follow-up time \(t_i\), the event indicator \(Y_i\) follows \[P(Y_i = 1) = w_p F(t_i; \mu_p, \sigma_p) + w_d F(t_i; \mu_d, \sigma_d), \quad F(t; \mu, \sigma) = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + \exp\{(\log t - \mu) / \sigma\}},\] where \(w_p = 1 / (k + 1)\) and \(w_d = k / (k + 1)\) for the randomization ratio \(k:1\), and \((\mu_p, \sigma_p)\) and \((\mu_d, \sigma_d)\) are the location and scale parameters on placebo and on the study drug. The hazard is decreasing when \(\sigma \ge 1\) and first increases and then decreases when \(\sigma < 1\). With the values \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) estimated from historical placebo data, the priors are \[\mu_p \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(PT_{HP} \mu / DF_p, PT_{HP} / DF_p), \quad \sigma_p \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(PT_{HP} \sigma / DF_p, PT_{HP} / DF_p),\] \[\mu_d \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\mu, 1), \quad \sigma_d \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\sigma, 1),\] with the shape and rate parameterization. The priors of the placebo parameters have the means \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), and \(PT_{HP} / DF_p\) sets their precision; the priors of the study drug parameters are weakly informative.

Duncan (2026) does not state which relative risk is used for the signal criterion of this model. bssd uses the ratio of the cumulative incidences at a time \(t^*\), \[RR(t^*) = F(t^*; \mu_d, \sigma_d) / F(t^*; \mu_p, \sigma_p),\] and declares a signal when \(P\{RR(t^*) > \theta_c \mid \mathrm{data}\} > P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}\).

The arguments of llbern_post() correspond to the symbols as follows.

Symbol Argument Description
\(Y_i\) y event indicator of each subject (1 if the subject had the event during follow-up)
\(t_i\) t follow-up time of each subject
\(k\) k randomization ratio of study drug to placebo
\(\mu\), \(\sigma\) mu_hp, sigma_hp log-logistic parameters estimated from the historical placebo data
\(PT_{HP}\) pt_hp total patient time of the historical placebo data
\(DF_p\) df_p discount factor
mu_d_prior, sigma_d_prior shape and rate of the priors of \(\mu_d\) and \(\sigma_d\) (defaults c(mu_hp, 1) and c(sigma_hp, 1))
\(t^*\) t_star time at which the relative risk and the cumulative incidences are evaluated
\(\theta_c\) rr0 critical value of \(RR(t^*)\) (default 1)
\(P_{\mathrm{cutoff}}\) cutoff posterior probability threshold (default 0.95)

The parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) refer to the time unit of t and t_star. ll_cdf() computes \(F(t; \mu, \sigma)\), and ll_mu() gives the location parameter for a cumulative incidence at a given time.

Example

The following data are simulated with sim_blinded(): 150 subjects randomized 1:1 with uniform entry over 26 weeks, up to 104 weeks of follow-up, and log-logistic times to the event with \(\sigma = 0.8\). The cumulative incidence at week 104 is 3.5% on placebo (\(\mu_p = 7.3\)) and 12% on the study drug, whose location parameter is obtained with ll_mu(). The blinded analysis is at week 117.

set.seed(2026)
mu_d <- ll_mu(0.12, t = 104, sigma = 0.8)
mu_d
#> [1] 6.238335
d <- sim_blinded(n = 150, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 104,
                 analysis_time = 117, dist = "loglogistic",
                 par_p = c(7.3, 0.8), par_d = c(mu_d, 0.8))
c(subjects = nrow(d), events = sum(d$event))
#> subjects   events 
#>      150       10

The priors use the placebo parameters as mu_hp and sigma_hp, and a historical placebo group of 75 subjects followed for 104 weeks (150 patient-years) discounted by \(DF_p = 2\), as in the simulations in the folder reproduce of the installed package. The relative risk is evaluated at the end of follow-up, \(t^* = 104\) weeks.

fit <- llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
                   sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = 75 * 104 / 52, df_p = 2,
                   t_star = 104)
fit
#> Model: LL_BERN 
#> Relative risk: ratio of cumulative incidences at t_star = 104 
#> P(RR(t_star) > 1 | data) = 0.6967
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): no
#> Posterior of RR(t_star): mean 3.205, median 2.097, 95% interval (5.798e-28, 13.52)
#> Cumulative incidence at t_star = 104: placebo 0.04739, study drug 0.08356, difference 0.03616
summary(fit)
#>     model      prob signal  rr_mean rr_median     rr_lower rr_upper ip_placebo
#> 1 LL_BERN 0.6966964  FALSE 3.204699  2.096947 5.798076e-28 13.52066  0.0473919
#>      ip_drug ip_difference       error
#> 1 0.08355556    0.03616366 0.001012859

The posterior probabilities for other critical values of \(RR(104)\) are obtained with rr0; details = FALSE skips the quantiles and control = list(check = FALSE) skips the repeated computation for the error estimate:

vapply(c(1, 1.5, 2), function(q) {
  llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
              sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = 75 * 104 / 52, df_p = 2,
              t_star = 104, rr0 = q, details = FALSE,
              control = list(check = FALSE))$prob
}, numeric(1))
#> [1] 0.6972028 0.6041112 0.5161246

The posterior distribution of \(RR(t^*)\) can have a heavy right tail, so the posterior median is a more stable summary than the posterior mean.

Numerical integration

llbern_post() integrates the four-dimensional posterior numerically on the coordinates \(\log \mu_p\), \(\log \sigma_p\), \(\log \mu_d\) and the prior distribution function of \(\sigma_d\). A coarse grid locates the region that holds almost all posterior mass. Gauss-Legendre quadrature is used for three coordinates and Chebyshev interpolation for \(\log \mu_d\); because \(RR(t^*) > \theta_c\) holds exactly when \(\mu_d\) is below a value determined by the other three parameters, the posterior probability is obtained from the cumulative integral of the interpolant (see ?llbern_post). With control$check = TRUE, the default, the computation is repeated on a finer grid, the finer result is returned, and twice the absolute difference in prob is reported as the error estimate (fit$integration$error, here 1.0e-03). The factor two is explained in ?llbern_post: when there are few events, the error decreases slowly as the grid is refined. The error estimate can be reduced by increasing control$n_inner.

The script inst/validation/validate_convergence.R compares the default grid with a much finer grid for the following data sets. For L1, whose posterior of \(\sigma_d\) has much mass near zero, both are also compared with an independent reference computed in Python (inst/validation/python/ref_llbern_breakpoints.py). The column Error estimate is the error estimate reported with the default grid.

Comparison with MCMC

The script inst/validation/validate_jags.R compares llbern_post() with MCMC in JAGS for the simulated data sets below. The JAGS model is written directly from the model specification of Duncan (2026, Section 3.4) and shares no code with bssd:

model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    pp[i] <- ilogit((log(t[i]) - mu_p) / sigma_p)
    pd[i] <- ilogit((log(t[i]) - mu_d) / sigma_d)
    y[i] ~ dbern(wp * pp[i] + (1 - wp) * pd[i])
  }
  mu_p ~ dgamma(s1, r1)
  sigma_p ~ dgamma(s2, r2)
  mu_d ~ dgamma(s3, r3)
  sigma_d ~ dgamma(s4, r4)
}

The results in this section are read from the output of that script (validate_jags.csv in the folder validation/results of the installed package); JAGS is not run when this article is built.

L1 150 1 9 (7.3, 0.8) (6.1, 0.8) 3.5% / 13.9% 104 117.0 (7.3, 0.8) 1
L2 200 1 30 (6.17, 1.6) (6.17, 1.6) 20.0% / 20.0% 52 34.7 (6.17, 1.6) 1
L3 100 1 3 (7.3, 0.8) (7.3, 0.8) 3.5% / 3.5% 104 78.0 (7.3, 0.8) 1

The data are simulated with sim_blinded() with the placebo and study drug parameters, and the relative risk and the incidences are evaluated at the end of follow-up (\(t^*\)); the script gives the other settings. JAGS was run with 4 chains, 5,000 burn-in iterations and 50,000 iterations per chain. The Monte Carlo standard error (SE) of each MCMC estimate uses the effective sample size of the draws (coda::effectiveSize()); for the posterior probabilities, the effective sample sizes are between 38,816 and 75,628. For the median, the table shows the MCMC proportion of draws below the posterior median of \(RR(t^*)\) computed by bssd, which should be 0.5. The incidences are the posterior means of the cumulative incidences at \(t^*\). The column Ratio is the absolute difference divided by the SE.

In all 12 items, the bssd value is within 1.2 standard errors of the MCMC value, and 12 items are within two standard errors. The largest absolute difference in a posterior probability is 0.0030, while the SEs of the MCMC probabilities are between 0.0017 and 0.0025. The integration error estimates of bssd for these data sets are between 2.5e-04 and 1.1e-03. Differences of this size are expected from the Monte Carlo error of MCMC alone, so the difference between the numerical integration of bssd and MCMC is negligible in practice. The validation script judges an item PASS when the difference is at most four standard errors; 12 of the 12 compared items are PASS.

References
